topic: Corporate, Securities, and Commercial Law: Company Law 2013
description: This module covers the fundamentals of the Companies Act, 2013. It focuses on the distinct legal personality of a company, the doctrine of piercing the corporate veil, types of companies, and the foundational documents: Memorandum of Association (MoA) and Articles of Association (AoA).

key_points: Separate Legal Entity: Established in the landmark case of Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd., a company is a distinct legal person separate from its shareholders and directors. It can own property, sue, and be sued in its own name.
Limited Liability: A fundamental advantage of incorporation. The liability of members is generally limited to the unpaid amount on their shares or the amount they have guaranteed to contribute.

Piercing the Corporate Veil: The law generally protects members under the corporate veil. However, courts can 'lift' or 'pierce' this veil and hold the individuals behind the company personally liable if the corporate form is being used for fraud, tax evasion, or as a mere sham/cloak for illegal acts.

Private Company (Section 2(68)): Restricts the right to transfer its shares, limits the number of its members to 200, and strictly prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe to its securities.

Public Company (Section 2(71)): A company which is not a private company. It has no restriction on the transferability of its shares, requires a minimum of 7 members (with no maximum limit), and can raise capital from the public.

One Person Company (OPC): A revolutionary concept introduced in the 2013 Act. It allows a single individual to form a company with limited liability, promoting entrepreneurship for sole proprietors without needing a second member.

Memorandum of Association (MoA): The charter or constitution of the company. It defines the company's scope, objectives, and powers. Any act undertaken by the company that is beyond the scope of its MoA is 'ultra vires' (beyond powers) and void.
Articles of Association (AoA): Contains the internal rules, regulations, and bye-laws for the internal management and administration of the company.

Doctrine of Indoor Management: Originating from the Royal British Bank v. Turquand case, this doctrine protects outsiders dealing with the company in good faith. It allows outsiders to assume that the internal proceedings of the company (as required by the AoA) have been properly complied with by the directors.

questions.question: Which landmark English case firmly established the principle that a registered company is a separate legal entity distinct from its members and shareholders?

options.C: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.

questions.explanation: Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd. (1897) is the cornerstone case in company law that established the doctrine of separate corporate personality, meaning a company exists as an independent legal person distinct from its founders and shareholders.

questions.question: Rohan wants to incorporate a startup. He wants to ensure that the shares cannot be freely traded by the public to prevent hostile takeovers, and he wants to cap the maximum number of members at 200. Which type of company should he incorporate under the Companies Act, 2013?
questions.explanation: According to Section 2(68) of the Companies Act, 2013, a Private Company is specifically defined by three restrictions: it restricts the right to transfer its shares, limits the maximum number of members to 200, and prohibits public invitations to subscribe to its securities.

questions.question: A company's Memorandum of Association (MoA) explicitly states that its sole business objective is to manufacture leather shoes. The Board of Directors signs a massive contract to buy land to start a cement factory. Later, the company refuses to pay the seller. Can the seller legally enforce this contract against the company?

options.A: Yes, because of the Doctrine of Indoor Management which protects the seller.
options.B: Yes, because the directors signed it as authorized agents of the company.
options.C: No, because the contract is 'ultra vires' (beyond the powers) of the company's MoA and is absolutely void.
options.D: No, because land purchases always require unanimous shareholder approval.

questions.explanation: The Doctrine of Ultra Vires states that any act done by a company which is outside the scope of the 'objects clause' in its Memorandum of Association is wholly void and completely ineffective in law. It cannot be ratified even if all shareholders agree, meaning the seller cannot enforce the contract against the company.
